stops.name: Coupvray, the birth house on the rue des Buttes (13 rue Louis Braille)
stops.campa: On the fourth of January a boy is born in the low stone house among the vines east of Paris, fourth child of Simon-René Braille, master saddler, and Monique Baron. The Marne runs below, the coach road to Germany passes above. The ground floor is the workshop: bridles and traces hung on the walls, the smell of tanned hide and beeswax, awls and knives ranked on the bench. Into this house of leather and light the child comes with two seeing eyes, and the whole village of Coupvray goes about its winter work unknowing that a new alphabet has entered the world.

stops.name: Church of Saint-Pierre, Coupvray: the baptism
stops.campa: Two days old, the infant is carried across the square to Saint-Pierre and christened at the font that still stands there. The Abbé Pillon, who will die before the boy is grown, pours the water; the parish register takes his name. He is a child of this stone and this bell, of the priest and the schoolmaster and the vine. All his life he will keep the faith received here at the font, and on his deathbed forty-three years hence he will call it back to himself as the one thing certain.

stops.name: The workshop, the awl that slips (Simon-René's atelier)
stops.campa: He is three, and the workshop is his kingdom. Left alone among the tools, he takes up an awl and a scrap of hide and does what he has watched his father do a thousand times: leans in, squinting close, and drives the point down hard to pierce the leather. The tough hide turns the blade; the awl leaps upward and enters his eye. The house fills with a child's cry. This is the wound that is the origin: from the small bright pain in the leather-smelling dark, the whole future of reading fingers begins. The village doctor comes, then a surgeon from Paris; neither can undo it.

stops.name: Coupvray, the infection crosses, and the dark closes (sympathetic ophthalmia)
stops.campa: The wounded eye festers for weeks, and then the sound eye, in sympathy, begins to cloud: the strange mercy-less mirroring the physicians will one day name sympathetic ophthalmia, one eye following the other into ruin. Slowly, through his fourth year and his fifth, the light withdraws. By five he sees nothing at all. The family speaks of it gently, and he learns to move by sound and touch through the house he still remembers seeing. He is not told he is blind so much as he discovers, room by room, that the visible world has become a thing to be reached for.

stops.name: The village school of Coupvray, learning by ear (Abbé Palluy, Antoine Bécheret)
stops.campa: The new curé, the Abbé Jacques Palluy, marks the blind boy's quickness and takes him under his teaching; soon he has nothing left to give him and carries an unheard-of request to the schoolmaster Antoine Bécheret: let this sightless child sit among the seeing. Bécheret consents. Louis learns everything by ear, holding whole lessons in memory the others carry on paper, and outruns them all. Yet he can read not one word. He sits amid a roomful of letters he will never see, and the hunger that will drive his life is planted: to make the word itself something a finger can hold.

stops.name: The road to Paris, departure from Coupvray
stops.campa: In February, ten years old, he leaves the house of vines for the capital, riding the coach road he has heard rumbling above the village all his life. A scholarship carries him: the intelligence the abbé saw, now vouched for on paper. Behind him the Marne, the workshop, the church, the mother's kitchen; ahead the city and a school for children like himself, of whom until now he has known none. It is the great parting of his life: he will come back to Coupvray only in summers, and at the last in a coffin.

stops.name: Institution Royale des Jeunes Aveugles, rue Saint-Victor (Séminaire Saint-Firmin)
stops.campa: He enters the Royal Institute for Blind Youth, lodged in the old Séminaire Saint-Firmin on the rue Saint-Victor, a damp, crumbling house near the Seine where the founder Valentin Haüy had first proved that the blind could be taught. The rooms are cold and unhealthy; tuberculosis walks the corridors and will one day take him. But here he finds his people: Gabriel Gauthier, Hippolyte Coltat, friends for life. Here too he meets the thing that will define him: books the blind can read, and their terrible insufficiency.

stops.name: The embossed library, Haüy's raised Roman letters
stops.campa: They set the great books before him: Haüy's invention, ordinary Roman letters pressed in relief into heavy paper so the finger may trace their shapes. The whole library holds but fourteen titles. Each volume is vast and fragile and dear; each word must be spelled out letter by laborious letter, the fingertip crawling over serifs and curves built for the eye, not the hand. He reads them all. And reading them he understands the flaw at the root: a script made for seeing can never be swift for touching. The blind deserve an alphabet of their own.

stops.name: The music room, cello and organ under Jean-Nicolas Marrigues
stops.campa: At the Institute music is not ornament but a trade the blind may practice among the sighted, and Louis takes to it as to his native tongue. Under Jean-Nicolas Marrigues he learns cello and organ; his ear is exact, his memory bottomless. The manuals and stops become a second kind of reading: a world entered wholly through the hands. Already the question forms that will shape his invention: if the fingers can command all this music, why can they not as freely command all words? The organ loft and the alphabet grow in him together.

stops.name: The cipher arrives, Captain Charles Barbier's écriture nocturne
stops.campa: A retired artillery captain, Charles Barbier de la Serre, brings his 'night writing' to the school: sonography, a code of raised dots he devised so soldiers might read orders in the dark without a lamp to draw enemy fire. Twelve points in two columns, standing not for letters but for sounds. The Army had refused it. Barbier offers it now to the blind. To the boy Braille, twelve years old, it is a thunderclap. Not the shapes of the seeing pressed on paper, but pure points the finger takes in directly. The door he has been feeling for stands open.

stops.name: The flaw in the cipher, twelve dots too tall for the finger
stops.campa: He works Barbier's system to its limits and finds where it fails. The cell is twelve dots high, taller than the fingertip, so the finger must shift up and down and can never seize a sign at a single touch. And it spells sounds, not letters: no spelling, no punctuation, no numbers, no music, no way to write the words as they truly are. Braille sees that the idea is sound and the form is wrong. He begins, at twelve and thirteen, to cut it down, to fold the tall column into something the fingertip can cover whole.

stops.name: Coupvray summers, the boy inventing at his father's bench
stops.campa: Home for the holidays in the vine-country, he sits again at the workshop bench where the awl once fell, and there, the tradition holds, he takes up his father's tools not to make bridles but to make an alphabet. With an awl and a stylus he punches dots into paper hour upon hour, testing how few points the finger can tell apart at a touch, arranging and rearranging the cell. The instrument that blinded him becomes the instrument of his gift. What the awl took from one boy's eyes it gives back to millions of fingers.
